This is the complete transcription of the documentary episode **"Kingdom of Kush - History of Africa with Zeinab Badawi."**

***

**Zeinab Badawi (Narrator):** Kush, in Northern Sudan, is one of the forgotten kingdoms of Africa and the ancient world. The Kings of Kush reached the zenith of their power in the 8th Century BC when they conquered their neighbor, Egypt. And their influence extended as far as the modern-day Middle East.

Sudan’s capital, Khartoum, is where the Blue and White Niles meet. The waters of the two rivers merge to form the mighty River Nile that flows through Northern Sudan into Egypt and ends its journey there, where it joins the Mediterranean Sea. The Blue Nile starts deep in the Ethiopian Highlands and the waters of the White Nile flow from Lake Victoria in East Africa, although it probably originates from deeper inside Central Africa.

The River Nile has for centuries played silent witness to the great civilizations that existed close to its banks. An unexpected game of football in the town of Karima in Northern Sudan. The youngsters laugh quite rightly at my lack of goalkeeping skills. Personally, I don’t think I’m that bad for a woman of a certain age. As I try to bridge the generation gap, so too does the town of Karima. It reaches down through the generations to a time long gone by when it was known as Kerma. And it is here that we begin the story of the Kingdom of Kush.

Early humans existed in Sudan for tens of thousands of years. By about 5000 BC, we know that people in Northern Sudan lived from fishing, hunting, and basic farming. And there’s evidence that they raised cattle too. They lived in relatively small, independent, and separate population groups. They had to be mobile so they could find good pasture for their livestock. The rich waters of the River Nile made the land fertile, which meant crops could grow easily, so farmers could settle down and develop communities.

The climate began to dry out gradually starting from about 5000 BC across North Africa, including what is today Sudan. This drove more people into the Nile Valley in search of hospitable land. It meant there were larger centers of population which became urbanized, and a hierarchy of chiefs or princes developed. By around 2500 BC, Kerma had become the center for the people who came to be known as the Kushites. Their buildings include large structures called *Deffufas*, which stood up to 18 meters high.

The ancient site of Kerma comprises two striking edifices, both built of sun-dried mud brick. They're known as the Western and Eastern Deffufa. Behind me is the Western Deffufa, which is believed to have been a temple. The Eastern Deffufa is a funerary chapel surrounded by a cemetery of mound graves.

**Dr. Abdelrahman Ali (Director of Sudan's National Museum):** The two Deffufas in Kerma are monumental mud-brick monuments. They belonged to the Kingdom of Kerma, which was known as the first independent national kingdom in the Sudan, developed in 2500 BC. The Kings of Kerma ruled Kerma for almost a thousand years. Kerma was known as the first and big urban center in sub-Saharan Africa. These two monuments were used as temples by the local community and the kings. In this monument, we could find the first indication of the utilization of the brick in the Nile Valley. An important fact about Kerma is that Kerma during that time acted as a national symbol and united all the tribes of the Sudan in one agglomeration.

**Zeinab Badawi:** We learn something about the inhabitants of Kerma from their death rituals, their customs, and what kind of objects they made and used. The traditional Kerma grave is marked by a dome-shaped tumulus of earth, outlined by a ring of black stones sprinkled over with white pebbles. The body was placed on the south side of the burial chamber. There was also pottery in the grave.

**Dr. Shadia Taha (Archaeologist):** Pottery is always abundant in all archaeological sites because it doesn't decay and it survives in all environments and climates. Pottery found in Sudan gave us information about the Neolithic groups who lived in Sudan at that time, Bronze Age groups, and Iron Age groups. We know a great deal about the clay they used, the techniques they used, the styles, the decorations... it tells us about the complexity of the ceramics, it tells us about trade and exchange. What we know now is that pottery was found in Sudan at 8000 BCE.

**Zeinab Badawi:** The National Museum in Khartoum has many exhibits from ancient Sudan. Between 1780 to 1580 BC, Kerma culture was vibrant. The people wore beautiful jewelry, they had bronze mirrors, stoneware, and delicate pottery. Some experts believe the ancient Sudanese were the first to develop the technique of enameling pottery.

This period of ancient Sudan's history is linked to that of its neighbor to the north, Egypt. At about the same time in ancient Egypt, that is around 3000 BC, the first dynasties were establishing the rule of the Pharaohs. What was the relationship like between these two close kingdoms? It was both hostile and complementary. And over the centuries, the balance of power would shift from one to the other. As Shadia Taha explains, in the writing of history mostly by Western scholars, the importance of ancient Sudan in this relationship has been rather overlooked.

**Dr. Shadia Taha:** Both countries influence each other, but the Eurocentric group always thought of Kerma as younger than Egypt and always copying Egypt. But they didn't give Kerma the credit it deserves, because Kerma was a very advanced state, and its civilization predated Babylon, Rome, and Greece. So the exchange of ideas went both ways; it wasn't just a receiver of ideas from Egypt.

**Zeinab Badawi:** When relations were bad, the Pharaohs of Egypt would launch raids into Kerma, and the people of Kerma also raided the Egyptians. However, when their relationship was good, trade flourished between the two kingdoms. Donkeys were used as pack animals. Unlike camels, they need a lot of water, so that supports the theory that at this time, the climate in Northern Sudan was more green and humid than it is today. As well as moving goods overland, they transported them along the Nile on boats that were later dismantled. The wood was reused in Egypt for building. But trade was hampered at certain times of the year when the Nile was impassable because of its cataracts.

There are six cataracts in the river. The first of them is here at this very spot in Aswan in Southern Egypt. The other five are in modern-day Sudan. As you can see, cataracts are rock formations in the river. And this meant that boats and ships would crash into them unless the waters of the Nile were high enough for them to avoid doing so. That meant for a large part of the year, the waters of the River Nile were not navigable, so traders would have to use overland routes, and this was more arduous and took a longer time.

Throughout history, the cataracts on the Nile gave the people of ancient Sudan a good natural defense from attackers coming by boat. Kerma laid the bedrock for the civilization of the Kushites.

**Dr. Shadia Taha:** Kush was well known for its very powerful army. They were very fierce archers, and the Egyptians called them "the Land of the Bow" because of their skills in the bow. So they know their ability and their strength and their power. In 1650, the Kushites ransacked Egypt, but they just went back. Kush was a powerful state and the Egyptians feared Kush.

**Zeinab Badawi:** So during this period of history, the Kushites succeeded in increasing their control of trans-African trade through the Sahara to the detriment of Egypt. For thousands of years, camel trains have made this journey from the south across the Sahara to Egypt. These camels are resting by the roadside and taking water in Dongola, in territory that would have been part of the Kingdom of Kush. Kush was a vital crossroads for trade in the ancient world, linking the West and the East in the Red Sea, and then from the South to the North in the Mediterranean.

The overland route through the hot terrain was difficult in the past and still is today. This man tells me they've ridden from Darfur in Western Sudan and are on their way to Cairo. That’s a distance of nearly 2000 kilometers.

Trade across land and along the Nile was, of course, a critical source of wealth, and so the Egyptians wanted to regain control of this trade route to restore their fortunes. By 1550 BC, ancient Egypt was at the start of a new Golden Age, and powerful rulers like Queen Hatshepsut and Thutmose III made it their mission to build up Egypt's trade again. Thutmose III sent an army up the Nile and defeated the people at Kerma. Now Egypt could take full advantage and exploit the kingdom's resources.

A new kingdom arose further south from Kerma in Napata, or Nabta as the Sudanese call it.

**Dr. Shadia Taha:** In my own opinion, they moved to Napata for economic, political, and religious reasons. Economic reasons because Napata was a meeting place for trade. The population was growing, they were already urban; they needed more resources. More resources were available in the south to supply an increasing population. And religious reasons: Jebel Barkal is the sacred mountain which Egyptians and Kushites believe that Amun resides in—the god Amun-Ra. So it is sacred for the Egyptians and the Kushites.

**Zeinab Badawi:** The Kushites' new kingdom at Napata is near the modern-day town of Karima by a mountain known today as Jebel Barkal. Their move coincided with another decline in Egypt, which had become so engulfed in its own internal rivalries that it paid little attention to Kush. This meant the kingdom at Napata, which began in El-Kurru, could develop undisturbed.

**Dr. Abdelrahman Ali:** As the civilization of Napata evolved from El-Kurru, it started as a small chiefdom and developed into a kingship and later on developed into an empire.

**Zeinab Badawi:** By the 8th Century BC, the Kings of Kush were growing ever richer and more powerful. At the Kushite capital of Napata, the mountain dominated the landscape, much as it does today. In its shadow, life goes on in El-Kurru. Time, I think, to abandon the open desert in search of human inhabitants. I want to get a feel for the kind of settlements that existed in the ancient Kingdom of Kush, and how far some of the ancient customs and practices still exist in modern-day Sudan.

I’ve been asking the ladies of the house to show me things which I know were used in the era of the Kushites and which I know are still used today. This is what's known as a *Zir*, and this was used in ancient times to keep water cool. It is absolutely fascinating that I can find an old house like this that is just so evocative of that period of Sudanese history. You can see the traditions of the Kushite kingdom still living on in the people who inhabit this area. People here eat the same grains and use similar earthenware storage urns. And the style of beds is one that has been in continuous use since ancient times. I remember beds like this from decades ago in the Sudan, but of course, people have since moved on and tend to use mattresses.

**Dr. Abdelrahman Ali:** The wooden bed has an important significance to the Sudanese community through the whole period from Kerma, from 2500 BC up to now. Because it has significance in daily life: for weddings, the ceremony started on a wooden bed—we call it *Angareb*—and even for the circumcision of the boys it was used. And finally, it was used to carry the deceased. If somebody dies, he will be carried to his final destination by a bed.

**Zeinab Badawi:** I’ve come across a wedding party in a settlement at the foot of Jebel Barkal. The men are gathered waiting for the ceremony to start. I reckon I can seize the chance to go and visit the women at the wedding breakfast, to see some female customs that have endured through the centuries. The bridegroom very helpfully takes me across the road to meet the ladies. I’m just looking at this lady's hands with the henna and the beautiful gold—two things that we had, of course, in the Kushite kingdom: the gold, and then, of course, the henna. The women of Kush dipped their hands in henna, decorated it, and they also wore kohl on their eyes like this lady here. And this is the holder that the kohl is kept in today. Amazing, she did it without any mirror!

Kushite women, like one famous princess who lived in the 8th Century called Amenirdis, wore elaborate jewelry. She probably had fine gold rings, bracelets, and colored beaded necklaces, like these in the National Museum, some made of ostrich eggshells. Amenirdis would have worn her hair flat to the head with a topknot, her long nails stained with henna, and her eyes darkened with kohl. So you can see the continuity of tradition is very much alive amongst the women at the wedding preparations. And you can also see it in the very masculine pursuit of wrestling, an activity which has stood the test of time.

The Kushites were renowned wrestlers and were held in highest esteem for their skill and fighting ability. Today in Sudan, especially in the Nuba Mountains in the southwest of the country, wrestling tournaments are held regularly. In days gone by, the Kushites would have engaged in such wrestling matches for sport. These local young men are clearly letting off a bit of steam as well as entertaining spectators.

By the early 8th Century BC, ancient Egypt’s fighting capability was much diminished. The country had grown weak and it could no longer ward off invaders. Egypt came under the rule of princes from Libya who had their own traditions and religion and had no regard whatsoever for those of the Egyptians. This was a source of great dismay for the Kushites. Through centuries of interaction, the Kushites had a religion and culture similar to the ancient Egyptians. They spoke their own Kushitic language, though they used Egyptian hieroglyphs for writing.

By 750 BC, the Kushites had had enough of the decadence of the Libyan princes and their allies in Egypt. At that time, Kush was ruled by a king called Kashta, and he believed it was his duty to save the Egyptians from further ruin. So he decided to invade Egypt. We don't have any depiction of Kashta, but presumably, he was not unlike the kings who succeeded him. Kashta’s ambitions in Egypt were limited; he simply wanted to protect the religious center of Thebes (modern-day Luxor) in southern or Upper Egypt. King Kashta was a force to be reckoned with. He owned the gold mines in Kush and controlled the River Nile and land routes for luxury goods like ebony and ivory from further south in Africa.

Kashta’s army was renowned for the skill of its horsemanship and its archers, who would dip their arrowheads in poison to make them more deadly. Their specialty was to shoot their opponents in the eye. Kashta’s army first took Thebes, the religious capital of Egypt. For the most part, the Kushites were welcomed by the locals there, grateful that their co-religionists were seeing off the heathen Libyans. With Thebes secured, Kashta could rest easy. Three years after he had begun the campaign into Egypt, King Kashta died. He was buried in El-Kurru in his homeland of Kush.

Kashta’s body was mummified in the Egyptian fashion and placed in a highly decorated wooden coffin covered in gold foil with inlays of colored glass and lapis lazuli. His body was placed facing east in the direction of which the sun rose, and the coffin was placed in a grave like this, above which a huge pyramid would have stood. As befits a dead king, Kashta would need a large number of grave goods for the afterlife. Pottery, personal ornaments, and jewelry were buried with him beneath his pyramid.

The Kushite pyramids differ from those in Egypt: they're smaller, steeper, and made of red sandstone. There are 1,000 pyramids that have been discovered so far in Sudan, though only about 300 of them are still standing as pyramid structures. In Egypt, there are about 100 pyramids. Our pyramids, the Sudanese pyramids, have different aspects because their angle of building is very steep compared to that of Egypt. We know that the kings and queens of Kush were buried with all manner of personal belongings and furniture, and also *shabtis*, which are these figures of people who would serve them in the afterlife.

Were they actually ever buried with real-life human beings?

**Dr. Abdelrahman Ali:** This is the idea of accompanying the deceased. Because in one grave in 1916, in one of the Kings of Kerma's grave, some of the deceased were parrying their faces with their hands. So it means that these people were maybe put into the grave intoxicated or drugged and put to accompany the king. In the later period, there is no indication of intentional accompanying of the king, but they put the *shabtis* to serve the king in the afterlife.

**Zeinab Badawi:** These pyramids here by Jebel Barkal are an example of how pyramids were looted both in antiquity and in centuries later to come. The tips of these pyramids are believed to have been covered in gold foil, where clearly now the tips have been destroyed and the gold removed. King Kashta’s reign as King of Kush had lasted around 13 years. However, it was his son Piye who was to take further the mission his father had started.

Piye was crowned king at the Temple of Amun in Jebel Barkal, probably in 747 BC, and he ruled for about 30 years until around 715 BC. Much of our knowledge of Piye comes from his stele, a massive slab of dark gray granite with 159 lines of text in Egyptian hieroglyphs known as the Victory Stele. It sets out how Piye first defeated and then ruled Egypt through establishing separate principalities. The stele begins with Piye's words:

*"Hear of what I did. I am a king, divine emanation, living image of Atum, who came forth from the womb adorned as a ruler, of whom those greater than he were afraid, whose father knew and whose mother recognized that he would rule."*

Under Piye, Egypt came further under Kushite control. However, when he heard about a key victory by his army, he was not content because some of the Egyptian princes had escaped to the north of the country. Piye vowed to go into battle himself, as recorded in his stele:

*"I shall make the Northland taste the taste of my finger."*

Piye pursued the Egyptian princes north and laid siege to them in their stronghold of Hermopolis. They eventually surrendered. After his victory, Piye searched through the palace for treasure. When he went into the stables and saw the horses had become emaciated during the siege, he was furious with the Egyptian prince:

*"I swear that as Ra loves me, as my nostrils are rejuvenated with life, it is more grievous in my heart that the horses have suffered hunger than any other evil deed that thou hast done in the prosecution of thy desire."*

The Kushites were excellent horsemen and prized their best specimens. As his favorite horses died off, Piye would have them buried near the royal tomb that had been built for him. On his return to Napata in Kush, Piye took with him architects and sculptors from Egypt, and he went about extending and reinforcing the Great Temple at Jebel Barkal. This is a computer-generated image of what the temple would have looked like. Piye ruled for nearly a decade after his campaign in Egypt. He died around 715 BC. Like other Kushite kings before him, King Piye was buried here at this site in El-Kurru, in a tomb surmounted by a pyramid built like this. In the centuries to come, his tomb was plundered, but we know that Piye was buried with many valuables. Fragments of furniture were found, a fine bronze stand, amulets bearing his name, and most importantly, four of his favorite horses were buried with him, entombed standing, their collars decorated with silver plumes and beads, to serve their master forever in the afterlife.

After Piye died, the throne passed to his younger brother, Shabaqo, who succeeded in conquering all of Egypt. He moved his capital to Thebes. By now, the powerful Kushites had attracted the attention of the warlike Assyrians who were threatening King Hezekiah of Judah. He appealed to Shabaqo for help, and he succeeded in warding them off. Kush was established as an African superpower.

When Shabaqo died in 702 BC, he was succeeded by his son Shebitqo, who again managed to see off the Assyrians. When Shebitqo died in 690 BC, the kingdom passed peacefully to his brother Taharqa. In the temples here at Jebel Barkal, you have these very rich decorations on the wall. And here on this wall, you have one of the greatest kings of Kush, Taharqa, making an offering of necklaces, probably gold, to the god Amun-Ra. After Thebes was defeated by the Kings of Kush, they assumed the style and the trappings of a Pharaoh, and they became Lord of the Two Lands.

Now to represent that, if you look at the top of Taharqa's head, he's got what are known as the twin uraei. A uraeus is the serpent shape that you can see representing Egypt and the land of Kush. And the Kings of Kush wore a tight-fitting crown which was actually a skullcap made of leather or metal with the sacred serpent symbols on them. There's a cord necklace falling over the shoulders or down the back. And the Kings of Kush are often depicted wearing a kilt. And the Kushites wore shoes or sandals—the poorest citizens went barefoot, but as a king, Taharqa's sandals would have been made of leather, usually with a high curved strap extending along the entire foot and curving over the toes to meet the soles. And on special occasions, their sandals might be colored in red, yellow, or green with decorations stamped on them in a snake pattern.

Like the kings before him, Taharqa was engaged in bloody rivalry with the Assyrians. This time, that’s around 670 BC, King Esarhaddon ruled Assyria. In their first military encounter, Taharqa defeated the Assyrians, but in a second battle in Egypt itself, the key city of Memphis fell to the Assyrians. Taharqa was wounded, and he withdrew from the battlefield and headed south to Thebes, where the Assyrians did not pursue him. Safe in Southern Egypt, Taharqa could embark on a huge building program, and the evidence is still clear at the Temple of Karnak today.

This column is the only one standing at its original height of the ten pillars built by Taharqa at Karnak. And this is yet further evidence of the impact of the Kushites' building program in ancient Egypt. The Sacred Lake at Karnak temple is a large rectangular basin, and its waters come from the River Nile. Although it was already here when the Kushites took control of Thebes, it owes its current shape to Taharqa. After an eventful life, Taharqa died probably in Egypt. But he wasn't buried in the royal cemetery at El-Kurru, but here in nearby Nuri. He chose the highest spot in the area for his pyramid, which is the biggest of those still standing. Some archaeologists believe that it was originally enclosed in a much bigger monument. Taharqa may not in the end have been able to prevent the Assyrian conquest of Memphis and the Nile Delta. The combined might of the Assyrians and their Egyptian allies proved too much for him. But his power and standing were recognized even many centuries after his death. In fact, he’s mentioned twice in the Bible.

After Taharqa’s death, the crown passed to his nephew Tanutamani. Tanutamani became king at what could hardly be described as an auspicious time; part of his kingdom was in the hands of the Assyrians and their Egyptian proxies. Tanutamani decided to go to Memphis, not far from modern-day Cairo, to try to reclaim the city for the Kushites. Tanutamani captured Memphis back from the Assyrians and restored his dynasty's glory. But his pride was short-lived. The Assyrians took the religious city of Thebes. They looted and utterly destroyed it. But deterred by the harsh climate, the Assyrians did not venture further south beyond Thebes and retreated.

The loss of Thebes severely undermined Tanutamani’s prestige. He returned to Kush humbled, but he remained king there until his death. His defeat by the Assyrians marked the end of Egypt's rule by the Kushite kings. They had formed the 25th Dynasty of the Pharaohs of Egypt, a period that had lasted nearly a hundred years. The balance of power now shifted back to Egypt.

The defeat of the Kushites in Egypt meant the sun had set on the Golden Era of the Kings of Kush. They never returned to Egypt, but they did continue to govern in Kush here in Northern Sudan for another thousand years. The Kushites built a new base called Meroë, about 250 kilometers north of Khartoum, an area known today as Al-Bagrawiya and not to be confused with the modern city of Merowe. This is the royal cemetery of Meroë. But it wasn't until the 3rd Century BC that the Kings of Kush were buried here.

The Kushites quickly developed a new and prosperous kingdom here. People began to farm as well as rearing livestock. And Meroë became a central point for commerce. An abundance of iron ore led to the working of iron.

**Dr. Shadia Taha:** Because metal at that time was very precious, they traded it. Their trade included Egypt, through Egypt to the Mediterranean. It went to India and China and to the rest of Africa. And that is why they became wealthy. Caravans and the trade in iron, beads, and glass and linen. Because they had the iron ore, they had the River Nile, they had water, and they had organization. Iron working in Meroë is equivalent to the Industrial Revolution in the West.

**Zeinab Badawi:** The royal family lived here at the Royal City. The buildings included a palace, a library, and baths. The Royal City is the best-preserved part of the ancient city of Meroë. All around you, you can see the remnants of buildings, monuments, and structures of a civilization that at its height enjoyed all the attributes of urban life. This would have been one of the finest tombs and pyramids at the Royal Cemetery in Meroë. It was for Queen Amanishakheto, who ruled Meroë at the end of the 1st Century BC. It was full of fine jewelry and other belongings to serve her in the afterlife. But her tomb was plundered by the Italian archaeologist Ferlini in the 19th Century. And after her baths, Queen Amanishakheto and other members of the royal family would just walk a few steps, come here, sit on one of these chairs, and enjoy a good massage.

The Queens of Kush at Meroë had a powerful role. Unlike the ancient Egyptians, women could succeed as monarchs in their own right, or they could rule jointly with their husbands or sons. And the king's relationship with his mother was of extreme significance.

**Dr. Shadia Taha:** Queen Amanishakheto, we know about her jewelry; she was covered in jewelry, and she used to love—well, all Kushite women loved gold and jewelry. She was a large lady. I have this muck which depicts her in most of the temples and the cemeteries as a very large woman. This is for two reasons: large ladies, it is a symbol of prosperity and a symbol of affluence. That means she was well-fed and she wasn't starved. The other thing I believe is because if you could see here in this muck, she is fighting an enemy who is shown as smaller than her, and she was really towering over him. So that could be another reason maybe exaggerating the size a little bit in these carvings. But they were still plump because it was a sign of power.

**Zeinab Badawi:** So they were powerful ladies. Queen Amanirenas actually fought the Romans—pretty powerful warrior queens, weren't they?

**Dr. Shadia Taha:** Yes, they led armies, and they used to go and really do lots of raids in Southern Egypt. So the fights between the Romans and the Kushites continued. Queen Amanirenas, in one of the battles, she was blinded in one eye, so she became the queen with one eye. And in the year 22 BCE, the Romans made a treaty which benefited the Meroites just to stop the fights between the two of them.

**Zeinab Badawi:** At Meroë, the Kushites embarked on a big building program. You can see here at the ancient site of Musawwarat clear evidence of temples and we think also palaces and other monuments. The Kushites interacted with other civilizations—ancient Romans, the Greeks also—and you can actually see this quite clearly in the influence, for instance, of ancient Greek architecture in this column here behind me.

Until the 2nd Century BC, the Kushites had written in ancient Egyptian. And then they introduced their own form of hieroglyphics, which is also pictographic like the ancient Egyptian one. And it is one of the great mysteries of the Kushites: we just simply cannot read their Meroitic language. We have an idea of what it might have sounded like, but we can't understand it. Why did the Kushites introduce their own hieroglyphics? Well, we believe it’s because the population formed in smaller groups and began to move around, and so they needed to communicate with one another.

The Meroitic era of ancient Sudan boasts many fine buildings, which showed the Kushites lived in some style in this period. In the mid-1st Century AD, King Natakamani and his wife Queen Amanitore were prolific builders at the site of Naqa. There were statues to Apedemak, the lion god. The Kushites worshipped the same gods as the ancient Egyptians; however, Apedemak was unique to them.

But the success and riches of Meroë attracted envy from a powerful new kingdom called Aksum in what we refer to today as the Horn of Africa. The Aksumites put Kush under pressure, contributing to its decline in the 4th Century AD. The fall of Kush meant a glorious chapter in the history of ancient Sudan and Africa came to an end. In the next program, we find out about the Kingdom of Aksum. What led to its rise and why it was described as one of the four great civilizations of the ancient world.
